strengths: Systematically explores an important and underexplored design space for synthetic stereo datasets, providing actionable findings on floating objects, backgrounds, materials, baselines, lighting, and render quality (Table 1).

Produces a new procedural generator and dataset, Infinigen-Stereo-150k, and demonstrates strong zero-shot stereo performance: DLNR-Infinigen-Stereo-150k achieves 3.76 on Middlebury 2014 (H) and 9.09 on Booster (Q), outperforming prior public checkpoints and a strong DLNR-Mixed baseline trained on 600k pairs from multiple synthetic datasets (Table 3).

Shows notable sample efficiency: just 500 random examples from Infinigen-Stereo outperform 100,000 CREStereo examples, and the data scales better with training budget than SceneFlow or CREStereo (Fig. 6).

Optimizes dataset generation cost substantially, reducing GPU render time from 3.37 minutes to 27 seconds per frame and CPU scene generation from 50.85 to 13 minutes while preserving downstream performance (Fig. 2, Sec. 3.3).
The paper is clear, well-structured, and provides extensive qualitative results and an appendix with assets and generation details, making the proposed pipeline understandable and likely reusable.

The contribution is practically useful: an open-source procedural generator and dataset can support further stereo matching research, especially for zero-shot generalization and synthetic-to-real transfer.
weaknesses: The parameter study is conducted at a reduced scale (5,000 stereo pairs, RAFT-Stereo, 75k steps). The paper asserts this is representative of full-scale training, but does not quantitatively validate that all conclusions transfer to the final 150k dataset, DLNR, or longer training regimes.

The final system removes many high-error materials and object types (e.g., highly transparent/reflective materials, thin structures) after manual inspection. This may limit dataset diversity and avoid hard cases that are important for real-world zero-shot generalization, even if it improves benchmark scores.

The final comparison table (Table 3) reports Booster only at quarter resolution and Middlebury 2014 only at half resolution, while full-resolution results are limited. This makes the strongest headline results less comprehensive than they could be.

The work is largely an engineering extension of Infinigen/Infinigen Indoors plus an empirical study; the core methodological novelty is moderate, and the paper does not compare against the original Infinigen generator or other recent procedural stereo datasets in the main quantitative tables.

Reproducibility cannot be fully verified at review time because the code and dataset are only promised for future release. Training details such as exact hyperparameters, random seeds, and baseline training schedules are not fully specified.

The paper lacks error bars or statistical significance analysis, which is relevant given the small-scale ablations and the relatively close differences between several parameter choices. Some claims, such as the abstract's emphasis on indoor floating objects, are also slightly at odds with Table 2, where the mixed dataset is best.

strengths: The paper provides a thorough and systematic empirical study of synthetic dataset design for zero-shot stereo matching, ablating many generator parameters such as floating object density, background objects, object type, material, stereo baseline, ray-tracing quality, lighting, and scene-type ratios with quantitative zero-shot evaluations (Tables 1-2, Fig. 4).

The proposed Infinigen-Stereo-150k dataset yields strong zero-shot results: DLNR-Infinigen-Stereo-150k achieves best or tied performance on Middlebury 2014/2021, ETH3D, KITTI 2012/2015, and Booster, outperforming a robust DLNR-Mixed baseline trained on 600k pairs from SceneFlow, CREStereo, TartanAir, and IRS (Table 3, Sec. 4.1).

The data-efficiency analysis is compelling: only 500 Infinigen-Stereo examples outperform 100,000 CREStereo examples, and performance continues to scale with more data while baselines plateau (Fig. 6).

The paper contributes practical dataset-generation optimizations that reduce rendering cost substantially, e.g., CPU time per indoor scene from 50.85 to 13 minutes and GPU rendering from 3.37 to 0.45 minutes with 1024 samples plus denoising (Fig. 2, Sec. 3.3), enabling construction of a 152k-pair dataset.

The work is reproducible and useful: the authors plan to open-source the generator, provide detailed procedural parameters, asset lists, ground-truth formats, and scene-type definitions (Appendix A), and evaluate on multiple standard benchmarks.

Qualitative results and error analysis show improvements on textureless regions and non-Lambertian surfaces (Figs. 5 and 7), and per-object/material analysis identifies problematic assets and motivates curation (Fig. 4).
weaknesses: The parameter study is performed at reduced scale (5k stereo pairs, RAFT-Stereo trained for 75k steps) and with a single architecture (RAFT-Stereo), so the selected design choices may not transfer to full-scale training or other stereo networks. The final dataset is validated with DLNR and RAFT, but each individual parameter choice is not re-validated at full scale.

Table 2 reports that a mixed dataset with equal parts indoor floating, dense floating, and nature (33-33-33) performs best, but the final Infinigen-Stereo-150k dataset uses approximately 45.6% indoor floating, 43.0% dense floating, and 11.4% nature. This discrepancy is not justified, weakening the claim that the final dataset incorporates the best ratio.

Some design choices prioritize generation cost over downstream performance: for ray-tracing quality, 8192 samples yields better zero-shot results (8.78/6.09 on Middlebury 2014 F/H) than 1024 samples plus denoising (9.19/6.60), yet the final dataset adopts the cheaper setting. This is a reasonable practical tradeoff but means the dataset is not strictly performance-optimized.

The system removes difficult objects and materials (e.g., cacti, urchins, racks, and highly transparent or reflective materials) based on high per-pixel error. While likely beneficial for label noise, this curation reduces coverage of challenging real-world cases and may limit robustness to thin structures and non-Lambertian surfaces; the strong Booster result partially mitigates this concern but does not fully address it.

The paper lacks a dedicated limitations section and does not deeply analyze failure cases of the final dataset or generator. It also does not clearly state whether the pre-generated Infinigen-Stereo-150k dataset itself will be released, as opposed to only the generation code, which affects exact reproducibility.

strengths: Systematic empirical study of procedural dataset design for zero-shot stereo matching, addressing a gap left by prior work that focused mainly on 2D flow datasets and stereo augmentations.

Introduces Infinigen-Stereo-150k and an open-source procedural generator; DLNR trained on this dataset outperforms DLNR-Mixed trained on 600k mixed synthetic pairs (e.g., 3.76 vs 5.21 on Middlebury 2014 H, 9.09 vs 12.17 on Booster) and improves over public zero-shot checkpoints.

Demonstrates practical cost optimizations (7.49x GPU rendering reduction, 3.9x CPU scene-generation reduction) with limited downstream performance loss, and shows strong sample efficiency (500 Infinigen examples beat 100k CREStereo examples in Fig. 6).
Thorough ablation of generation parameters (floating-object density/type, background objects, materials, stereo baselines, lighting, ray-tracing quality) with clear tables and figures.
Open-source code and a detailed appendix (ground truth, assets, generation details) support reproducibility and future research.
weaknesses: Limited architecture validation: the parameter study and final training use only RAFT-Stereo and DLNR; other state-of-the-art stereo networks (e.g., IGEV++) are evaluated only via public checkpoints, so generality across architectures remains unproven.

Ablation experiments use only 5,000 stereo pairs and 75k RAFT-Stereo training steps; no variance or multiple seeds are reported, and the claim that this reduced scale is representative is asserted rather than demonstrated.
Some final design choices are extrapolated beyond the ablation range (e.g., 200 objects for dense floating scenes, final scene-type ratio) without direct experimental validation in the paper.

Baseline training details are not fully specified (e.g., whether DLNR-Mixed uses identical training steps, masking, and schedule), leaving potential for unfair comparison; the 12%/14% RAFT claims appear to compare RAFT-Infinigen against DLNR-Mixed, an architecture mismatch.
Technical novelty is mostly in applying and tuning existing Infinigen generators for stereo rather than introducing a new stereo matching method or learning approach.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically important question: what aspects of synthetic stereo dataset design actually drive zero-shot generalization, rather than simply proposing yet another dataset.

Provides a systematic, quantified parameter study (floating-object density, background objects, object type, materials, lighting, stereo baseline, render quality) evaluated against standard benchmarks, giving the community actionable design guidance.

The resulting WMGStereo-150k dataset is shown to outperform training on a mixture of widely used datasets and to be competitive with FoundationStereo, and this is validated across multiple architectures (RAFT-Stereo, DLNR, Selective-IGEV), strengthening the generality of the findings.

Demonstrates strong sample efficiency (500 samples from WMGStereo-150k beating 100k CREStereo examples) and includes a practical cost-optimization study (denoising, solver realism, scene amortization) that makes large-scale generation tractable.
Includes a held-out evaluation (DrivingStereo, Midd-Train) that shows the dataset is not simply overfit to the benchmarks used for parameter tuning.
Open-sources the procedural generation code and parameter configurations, which is a meaningful contribution for reproducibility and for enabling future targeted dataset generation.
The paper is clearly written with informative figures (qualitative comparisons, per-object/material error analysis) and honest reporting of failure cases such as transparent/reflective materials.
weaknesses: The parameter study (Table 1) is conducted at a reduced scale (5,000 stereo pairs, 75k steps) while the final dataset uses different settings (e.g., 200 objects in dense floating scenes rather than the studied 0–30 range). The claim that the reduced scale is 'sufficiently representative' of full-scale training is only partially supported, so some conclusions may not transfer to the final regime.

The ablations vary each parameter independently against a fixed configuration rather than performing a full factorial design, so interactions between choices (e.g., object density vs. background realism vs. materials) are not fully characterized.

The comparison against 'Mixed' baselines uses a self-constructed mixture of prior datasets (600k pairs) rather than established published training recipes, and the improvements, while consistent, are relatively modest on some benchmarks (e.g., KITTI).

The dataset does not surpass FoundationStereo, and several findings (e.g., that floating objects and diversity help; that realism matters) largely confirm prior intuitions (Mayer et al.), limiting the conceptual novelty of the analysis.

The technical contribution in procedural generation builds heavily on existing Infinigen infrastructure, with the novel components being largely engineering (placement interfaces, material/object filtering), so the core methodological novelty is moderate.
Evaluation is restricted to zero-shot transfer; the practical benefit for models that are subsequently fine-tuned on real data (the common deployment setting) is not examined.
Some conclusions are explained only superficially (e.g., why background objects help despite prior claims that realism is overrated), leaving the underlying mechanism unclear.

strengths: Systematically investigates an underexplored question — what parameters of synthetic stereo training data actually matter — using a controlled procedural generator, filling a genuine gap that prior dataset papers (CRE, SceneFlow, TartanAir) never ablated.

The dataset contribution (WMGStereo-150k, 163k pairs) is well-supported: training solely on it outperforms training on a combination of SceneFlow/CRE/TartanAir/IRS by 28% on Middlebury and 25% on Booster (Tab. 2), and is competitive with FoundationStereo (Tab. 5), with demonstrated sample efficiency (Fig. 5) and held-out benchmark validation (Tab. 6) to guard against benchmark overfitting.
Open-sourcing the procedural generation code distinguishes this work from FoundationStereo (which provides no code/analysis) and makes the findings reproducible and extensible for the community.

The parameter study yields concrete, actionable findings (combining realistic indoor scenes with floating objects is best; background objects help; wide baseline range [0.04,0.4]m is best; diverse object types/materials are more robust; removal of transparent/reflective assets and thin-holed objects improves training), each backed by multi-benchmark numbers in Tab. 1 and the expanded EPE metrics in Tab. 7.

The cost-optimization study (Tab. 4, ray-tracing samples, solver realism, denoising, scene amortization) is a practical and often-omitted contribution that makes large-scale procedural data generation tractable.

Honest framing: the authors explicitly acknowledge the models are competitive with rather than superior to FoundationStereo, and that FoundationStereo implicitly used similar design choices; error analysis (Fig. 3) motivating asset removal is thoughtful.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: the system is built directly on top of Infinigen/Blender with incremental placement and augmentation interfaces, and the central recipe (realistic scenes + floating objects) is essentially the design already used by FoundationStereo. The paper reads more as a careful empirical study plus dataset than as a new technical method.

The parameter study is conducted under a reduced regime (5,000 pairs, 75k RAFT-Stereo steps), and the authors assert this is 'sufficiently representative' without fully validating it against the full-scale training regime; the best-setting conclusions could in principle shift at full scale.

The dataset does not surpass the current state of the art on most benchmarks (FoundationStereo remains better on nearly all columns of Tab. 2), so the headline value is a resource/analysis rather than a performance advance.

Several conclusions are explicitly benchmark-dependent (e.g., object-type choices trade off between Middlebury/KITTI/Booster, and 'only metal and glass' is best on KITTI/Booster but poor elsewhere), which weakens the generality of individual design prescriptions.

The lighting-augmentation conclusion is weak and somewhat speculative — the paper attributes the negligible effect to 'insufficient lighting variation in the benchmarks' without evidence, leaving this parameter's role unresolved.

The finding that scene realism matters somewhat contradicts Mayer et al. [20] ('realism is overrated'), but the paper does not deeply reconcile the two results beyond noting the difference in dataset style and disparity focus.
Generation cost is heavy (70.5 CPU-days + 120 GPU-days even after optimization), which may limit accessibility, though the optimizations and open code partly mitigate this.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored question. While prior work (Mayer et al. 2018; FoundationStereo) has touched on synthetic-data design, no stereo-specific study systematically isolates procedural generation parameters (floating-object density, background objects, object type, material, lighting, baseline). The ablation in Tab. 1 is a useful, controlled contribution.

The released dataset and open-source procedural generation code are a concrete community resource. As the authors correctly note, most existing stereo datasets (CRE Stereo, TartanAir, IRS, and even FSD) do not open-source their generation pipeline; providing a configurable generator plus an asset list (B.7) and GT construction details (B.4) is valuable for reproducibility and for follow-up work.

The dataset-comparison evidence is reasonably convincing in the places that matter. In Tab. 5, DLNR trained only on WMGSTereo-150k (5.10/3.76/6.72/2.50/3.30/4.54/9.09) beats SceneFlow, CREStereo, TartanAir and IRS across most benchmarks and is competitive with FSD. Fig. 5 shows sample efficiency (500 WMGSTereo samples beat 100k CREStereo samples on Middlebury), which is a meaningful practical property.

Findings generalize across architectures. Tab. 2 shows improvements for RAFT-Stereo, Selective-IGEV and DLNR when retrained on WMGSTereo-150k versus a Mixed baseline (e.g., DLNR 5.21→3.76 on Middlebury 2014 (H); Selective-IGEV 5.24→3.61), which supports the claim that the design findings are not model-specific.

The paper makes an effort to guard against benchmark overfitting by evaluating on held-out DrivingStereo and Middlebury-Train subsets (Tab. 6), and by using six benchmarks with standard metrics and thresholds.
weaknesses: Novelty and depth of insight are limited. The central conclusion — realistic indoor backgrounds combined with densely placed floating objects is best — is essentially the design already used by FoundationStereo's FSD and by several CRE Stereo-style datasets; the paper itself concedes FSD 'adopts similar settings to our final dataset.' Several other findings (more floating objects help; object/material diversity helps; a wide baseline range helps) are plausible a priori, so the contribution is largely confirmatory rather than surprising.

The ablations are run under a small, single-model budget (5,000 stereo pairs, 75k steps, RAFT-Stereo only, Tab. 1). The authors assert this reduced scale is 'sufficiently representative' but provide no verification that the rankings hold at full-scale training or for other architectures. Since some decision margins are small (e.g., Lighting 9.62 vs 9.19 on Middlebury 2014 H), it is unclear whether the chosen settings would survive a full training run.

No error bars or multi-seed runs are reported anywhere. For several ablations the differences are within a range that could plausibly be seed noise (e.g., material and lighting rows in Tab. 1), yet the paper picks winners and builds the final dataset on them. This weakens the reliability of the parameter conclusions.

Several ablations are inconclusive or degenerate. Lighting augmentation is reported to have 'little effect' (a null result that adds little). The material study is contradictory: 'only metal and glass' is best on KITTI-15 and Booster but worst on Middlebury/ETH3D, and the chosen 'all materials' setting is effectively the default, so the ablation does not yield a clean actionable finding.

Table 2 conflates model comparison with dataset comparison. Retrained DLNR/Selective-IGEV/RAFT-Stereo are run for 200k steps on 163k pairs, whereas the 'prior methods' in the top block used their original schedules/data. Part of the apparent gain over prior methods is therefore attributable to longer retraining and stronger base models rather than to the dataset itself. Table 5 is the cleaner comparison, and there the margin over FSD is not uniform (FSD is better on Middlebury H, ETH3D, KITTI-12 and Booster).

Comparisons to FoundationStereo are not apples-to-apples: FSD is a much larger model trained on a much larger corpus, and the paper acknowledges it 'performs worse than FoundationStereo' yet still frames results as 'state-of-the-art' competitive. The 'state-of-the-art' framing is overstated relative to the actual numbers.

The dataset quality is validated only through downstream benchmark px-error/EPE. There is no direct assessment of GT depth/disparity accuracy, occlusion-map correctness, or failure cases in the released data, which is important for a dataset paper whose central artifact is the data itself. Generation cost is also very high (~70.5 CPU-days + 120 GPU-days), limiting practical reuse despite the cost-optimization section.

Minor issues: the dataset is named WMGSTereo-150k but contains 163,666 pairs; and the title/abstract framing ('we investigate... and report the effects') sets expectations for a broader study than the six indoor-oriented parameters actually examined (e.g., no analysis of resolution, frame count, or outdoor/driving scene design, which the benchmarks heavily weight).
